avoid: inventing a Russian acronym or translating the letters -- 'LEGB' is the term working Python developers actually use and search for

Verified the course never attempts a Russian translation of the acronym itself -- correct, since 'LEGB' is the term a Russian-speaking developer would encounter in documentation, Stack Overflow, and job interviews.
terms.first_use_guidance: Keep 'LEGB' as a bare acronym; explain each letter in Russian but never replace the acronym itself.

avoid: 'закрытие' (a literal but semantically wrong calque -- reads as 'closing', not the functional-programming concept)
terms.rationale: build_chapter_13.py §13.13 uses 'замыкание' correctly and consistently for the nested-function-retains-enclosing-state concept (make_greeter/greet_anna example), explicitly flagging it as a term to recognize now with full treatment deferred to decorators later. 'Замыкание' is the standard, unambiguous Russian term used in Russian-language Python documentation and courses -- verified no confusion with the unrelated literal sense of 'closing'.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce 'замыкание' at first mention of a nested function outliving its enclosing call; note explicitly that full treatment (decorators) comes later, exactly as the course already does.

terms.preferred_ru: параметры только по имени (keyword-only) / только по позиции (positional-only)
avoid: translating 'keyword-only'/'positional-only' into a single unclear Russian phrase without keeping the English term visible -- the syntax markers (bare * and /) are themselves language-agnostic and readers will meet the English names in real documentation
terms.rationale: build_chapter_13.py §13.9 teaches the bare-* and bare-/ syntax with a three-zone capability_map ('только позиционно' / 'позиционно ИЛИ по имени' / 'только по имени'). Verified the course keeps the English technical names present alongside the Russian description rather than replacing them outright, which matters because these exact English terms appear in Python's own error messages and PEP 570 documentation.
terms.first_use_guidance: Always pair the Russian descriptive phrase with the English term in parentheses on first use, since the English term is what appears in real tracebacks and docs.

avoid: 'сайд-эффект' (an unnecessary Runglish loanword when a precise, established Russian term already exists)
terms.rationale: build_chapter_13.py §13.11 defines both terms precisely (побочный эффект = функция меняет что-то ВНЕ своего возвращаемого результата; чистая функция = результат зависит только от аргументов) and explicitly frames both as legitimate function roles rather than one being universally superior. Verified this framing avoids the common overcorrection of presenting side effects as always-bad.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce 'побочный эффект' before 'чистая функция' (effect first, then its absence), matching the course's own sequencing, and explicitly state both are legitimate.

terms.preferred_ru: self (left as code; explicitly described as convention, not a reserved word)
avoid: presenting 'self' as a Python keyword or reserved word -- it is an ordinary parameter name that happens to be universal convention
terms.rationale: build_chapter_13.py §14.3 and §14.5 both explicitly call out 'self -- это не ключевое слово' (self is not a keyword) -- a callout box states it works even with a different parameter name but that using anything else would confuse every other Python reader. Verified this is factually correct (self is convention, not syntax) and the course states it twice for emphasis without contradiction.
terms.first_use_guidance: State explicitly on first use that self is a naming convention, not a language keyword -- this is a common beginner misconception worth pre-empting.

avoid: presenting Python's __name mangling as 'true privacy' -- the course explicitly and correctly debunks this ('в Python нет настоящей приватности на уровне языка')
terms.rationale: build_chapter_14.py §14.10 defines encapsulation precisely as hiding state behind methods that can validate new values, then correctly explains that _name and __name are conventions/name-mangling rather than language-enforced access control (schet._Konto__balans is shown working). Verified this avoids the widespread beginner-course error of claiming Python has 'private' attributes.
terms.first_use_guidance: Always pair 'инкапсуляция' with the explicit disclaimer that Python enforces this by convention (name mangling), not by language-level access control.

avoid: translating HAS-A/IS-A into Russian -- the course correctly keeps these as bare English mnemonics since they are the standard OOP vocabulary a developer will meet in any language's documentation
terms.rationale: build_chapter_14.py §14.13 and §14.15 both use the HAS-A/IS-A test as the practical way to choose between the two relationships (Uchastnik HAS-A turtle.Turtle, Sobaka IS-A Zhivotnoe), reinforced by relationship_diagram calls with style='has-a'/'is-a'. Verified the course explicitly warns against using inheritance just to 'borrow' methods without a genuine IS-A relationship -- correct OOP design guidance.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce the HAS-A/IS-A question as the practical test before naming which relationship (composition or inheritance) applies -- matches the course's own sequencing.

terms.preferred_ru: duck typing (left as the English term; described via the 'если это выглядит как утка...' idiom)
avoid: 'утиная типизация' as the primary form without keeping 'duck typing' visible -- both should appear, since 'duck typing' is what appears in real error discussions and interviews
terms.rationale: build_chapter_14.py §14.19 introduces the concept through the full English idiom and its literal Russian translation, then explicitly and correctly states 'полиморфизм не требует наследования' (polymorphism does not require inheritance) as the key misconception it corrects. Verified this term is genuinely bilingual in real Russian-language Python usage, so keeping both forms visible is the right call.
terms.first_use_guidance: Present the idiom in both languages on first use; do not silently drop the English 'duck typing' after the initial introduction.

terms.preferred_ru: специальные методы (дандер-методы as an accepted colloquial variant)
accepted_variants: дандер-методы (from 'double underscore'; used colloquially in the Russian-speaking Python community)
avoid: 'магические методы' (a widely-seen but discouraged calque of 'magic methods' -- the course correctly avoids implying anything mystical about a well-defined protocol)
terms.rationale: build_chapter_14.py §14.21 consistently uses 'специальные методы' as the primary Russian term and explains the double-underscore ('дандер', double underscore) etymology explicitly, never using 'магические методы'. Verified this is the more precise and increasingly standard choice in Russian-language Python material, since these methods follow a documented protocol rather than being 'magic'.
terms.first_use_guidance: Use 'специальные методы' as the default; 'дандер-методы' may appear as a secondary colloquial gloss, but never 'магические методы'.

terms.preferred_ru: dataclass (left as code/the decorator name; described as 'класс-данные' or 'класс для хранения данных')
avoid: implying @dataclass produces something other than a normal class -- the course explicitly and correctly debunks this misconception
terms.rationale: build_chapter_14.py §14.23 explicitly names and corrects two beginner misconceptions in one callout: '"dataclass -- это не настоящий класс" или "в dataclass нельзя писать методы" -- Оба неверны' (both are wrong). Verified @dataclass is accurately described as an ordinary class decorator that only adds generated __init__/__repr__/__eq__, with methods and properties working exactly as in any other class.
terms.first_use_guidance: Keep '@dataclass'/'dataclass' as code, glossed as 'класс-данные'; explicitly state it remains a normal class on first use.

avoid: using only informal phrasing ('сохранить в файл') without the precise terms -- the course explicitly introduces the precise vocabulary via a dedicated callout
terms.rationale: build_chapter_15.py §15.24 defines both terms precisely in a dedicated callout ('Сериализация -- превращение структуры Python... в представление, которое можно сохранить или передать... Десериализация -- восстановление структуры данных обратно') before the JSON/CSV sections that use the concept repeatedly. Verified both Russian terms are the standard, unambiguous ones used throughout Russian-language software engineering material.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce both terms together, before the first concrete format (JSON), exactly as the course does.

terms.preferred_ru: текущая рабочая директория (CWD as an accepted bare acronym)
accepted_variants: CWD (used bare after first introduction, matching real tooling/documentation)
avoid: conflating CWD with 'the folder where the script file lives' -- the course dedicates an entire section and a Debug Lab specifically to correcting this exact misconception
terms.rationale: build_chapter_15.py §15.7 states the distinction as a callout ('CWD -- это НЕ "папка со скриптом"') and reinforces it with Debug Lab 2, showing a FileNotFoundError that results from confusing CWD with the script's own directory. Verified this is one of the most common real-world path bugs, and the course's terminology and worked example are both accurate.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce 'текущая рабочая директория' with its acronym CWD together, and immediately contrast it with 'папка со скриптом' to pre-empt the standard confusion.

avoid: describing mainloop()/the event loop as the program 'freezing' or 'waiting idly' -- the course explicitly and repeatedly corrects this exact misconception
terms.rationale: build_chapter_16.py §16.1 and §16.9-16.10 introduce 'событийно-ориентированное программирование' as the term for GUI control flow, contrasted directly against the sequential terminal model, with repeated explicit callouts that mainloop() is 'не "замирание", а цикл обработки событий' (not freezing, but an event-processing loop). Verified the term and its contrast with sequential execution are both accurate and consistently reinforced across the chapter's opening and closing sections.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce the term by direct contrast with the terminal's sequential model (глава 1-15), not in isolation -- matches the course's own §16.9 structure.

avoid: 'элемент управления' as the primary term -- 'виджет' is what Russian-speaking Tkinter/GUI developers actually say and is used consistently by the course itself
terms.rationale: build_chapter_16.py §16.2 and §16.11 define 'виджет' as any visible/interactive interface object and build a whole dedicated section around the widget tree (each widget has a parent/master except the root). Verified the course uses 'виджет' as a fully naturalized loanword throughout the chapter without ever reaching for a native-Russian paraphrase, matching real Russian-language Tkinter/GUI-framework usage.
terms.first_use_guidance: Use 'виджет' from first mention without translation; the course's own definition ('любой видимый/интерактивный элемент интерфейса') can serve as the one-line gloss on first use.

accepted_variants: bind()
avoid: биндинг
terms.rationale: The chapter's central new mechanism, explicitly contrasted with command= (Ch. 16) as a distinct, more general way to react to events.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce paired with command= to make the contrast concrete.

accepted_variants: фокус
terms.rationale: Introduced in Ch. 17 and immediately load-bearing for focus_get()/focus_set() and keyboard-event handling.
terms.first_use_guidance: Gloss once at first use, then use bare.

terms.rationale: The chapter's most repeated architectural phrase, distinguishing the state model from what widgets display.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce when separating GameState from widgets.

accepted_variants: Canvas (виджет)
avoid: канвас
terms.rationale: Consistent for both the Tkinter widget and its drawing surface; never calqued.
terms.first_use_guidance: No gloss needed after first introduction.

accepted_variants: item ID
terms.rationale: Central to the chapter's mental model: Canvas stores retained items (not pixels), each with an integer id that is not a Python id().
terms.first_use_guidance: Explicitly contrast with Python's own id() the first time it appears.

avoid: z-order (без перевода)
terms.rationale: The chapter's Russian rendering for how later-created Canvas items render above earlier ones; z-order stays as the English equivalent, not the primary term.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce with tag_raise/tag_lower.

terms.rationale: One discrete step of game-state update, distinct from the game loop that repeats it.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce before the real timer-driven loop (19.13).

terms.rationale: The event-driven repetition mechanism (screen.ontimer in Turtle, the frame loop in Pygame); used consistently across the two game-project chapters.
terms.first_use_guidance: Distinguish a busy/blocking loop (anti-pattern) from the real timer/frame-driven loop from first use.

accepted_variants: вектор смещения (dx, dy)
terms.rationale: Represents movement as a (dx, dy) pair rather than four separate boolean flags; central to the grid/vector model.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce alongside the grid-as-coordinates model.

terms.rationale: The dataclass holding all mutable game data is distinct from the enum describing which phase the game is in; the chapter is careful to keep the two separate.
terms.first_use_guidance: Name both terms together the first time GameState/GameStatus appear.

terms.rationale: Pygame chapter deliberately distinguishes one iteration of the game loop from one frame of a sprite's animation sequence -- the one real terminology collision risk in this vocabulary, worth keeping apart.
terms.first_use_guidance: Name the distinction explicitly the first time animation frames are introduced.

avoid: дельта времени
terms.rationale: Kept in Latin script with dt as the code identifier, matching real Russian Pygame-community practice; never translated in prose.
terms.first_use_guidance: Gloss once as 'время, прошедшее с прошлого кадра', then use dt bare.

terms.rationale: Standard Russian gamedev term; the chapter uses it primarily as 'image object' rather than pygame.sprite.Sprite specifically -- worth noting both senses exist.
terms.first_use_guidance: Note the general-image-object sense is what this course teaches, distinct from the pygame.sprite.Sprite class.

terms.rationale: Established transliteration in Russian gamedev for the simplified collision rectangle; AABB kept as the acronym with a one-time gloss.
terms.first_use_guidance: Gloss AABB once on first use.

terms.rationale: Distinguishes the game's logical coordinate space from actual pixel positions on screen; explicitly scoped as 'not needed for this book's projects' rather than left ambiguous.
terms.first_use_guidance: Introduce alongside Rect, note it is out of scope for the book's own projects.
